children: Manmohan Sharma says despite margin pressures in the second quarter of FY27, Waaree Renewable Technologies remains optimistic about its growth prospects, backed by a strong order book, expansion in transmission and distribution, and rising demand for renewable energy infrastructure

Waaree Renewable Technologies (WRTL) reported a 37 per cent increase in consolidated revenue in Q2 FY27, even as profit after tax declined nearly 30 per cent. The company is expanding beyond solar engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) into transmission and distribution (T&D), supported by its acquisition of Associated Power Structures.

In an exclusive interaction with BW Businessworld, Manmohan Sharma, Chief Financial Officer, Waaree Renewable Technologies, discusses the company's profitability, order execution, diversification strategy and the outlook for India's renewable energy sector. Edited excerpts:

Revenue grew 37 per cent in Q2, but profit after tax declined nearly 30 per cent. How much of this margin pressure is temporary, and what would be a sustainable margin for WRTL following diversification?

The reduction in margins is primarily due to the blending of our transmission and distribution business with solar EPC operations. Our solar EPC business also did not perform as strongly during the quarter as it has in previous periods.

However, we received approximately 1.7 GW of orders during the quarter. With an unexecuted solar EPC order book of around Rs 3,300 crore, we expect these orders to translate into revenue over the coming quarters.
Solar EPC revenue declined year-on-year despite consolidated revenue growth. Is this an execution timing issue or a structural change in the growth profile of the business?
It is purely a timing-related issue and temporary for this particular quarter. We have a strong order book that is expected to be executed over the next few quarters.

We expect the existing orders to convert into revenue as execution progresses. This should be one of those quarters where such a situation has occurred, rather than an indication of a structural change in the business.

Transmission and distribution contributed more than Rs 600 crore in revenue during the quarter following the acquisition of Associated Power Structures. How quickly can this business scale, and how significant could its contribution become?

The transmission and distribution business generated close to Rs 2,000 crore in revenue during the previous financial year and approximately Rs 600 crore during the current quarter. It also has an order pipeline of around Rs 2,200 crore, which is expected to translate into revenue over the next few quarters.

The existing galvanising and processing capacity is approximately 1.08 lakh metric tonnes per annum. We are initiating an expansion to more than double this capacity to over two lakh metric tonnes annually. This expansion should take shape over the next two to three quarters.

India needs more transmission and distribution infrastructure to evacuate power from both solar and conventional generation sources. By expanding our capacity and securing additional orders, we expect this business to contribute significantly to the company's overall revenue.
There is also scope to improve the margin profile of the business through integration and operational improvements over the coming quarters.
With more than Rs 5,500 crore in unexecuted orders, how much revenue visibility does the current order book provide for the remainder of FY27 and FY28?
The order book comprises approximately Rs 3,200 crore in solar EPC orders and Rs 2,200 crore in transmission and distribution orders.
We expect these orders to be executed over the next three to four quarters. New orders received during the coming quarters will also contribute to revenue across both businesses.

There is substantial visibility in terms of opportunities available in the renewable energy sector. Solar accounts for more than 171 GW of India's installed renewable energy capacity, and the continued expansion of the sector creates opportunities for both solar EPC and transmission infrastructure.
We expect these businesses to grow over the coming quarters and the next few years.

WRTL has a pipeline of over 34.6 GWp in solar, 12.5 GWh in battery energy storage systems and more than Rs 21,900 crore in transmission and distribution. Where do you see the strongest combination of growth and profitability over the next three years?
Our solar pipeline includes approximately 25 GW of domestic opportunities and 9 GW in overseas markets.

We have started actively participating in opportunities in the Middle East, while continuing to receive repeat orders from existing customers in India. We are also pursuing bilateral opportunities and expect to close some orders in the coming quarter.
There are significant opportunities in both solar EPC and transmission and distribution. These are essential infrastructure segments, and we expect demand to continue over the coming years.

Q2 results across renewable energy companies indicate strong capacity additions and revenue growth, but also margin pressure in parts of the EPC and manufacturing value chain. Is the industry entering a phase where execution profitability matters more than capacity expansion?
We have always followed a disciplined approach to profitability. We do not accumulate orders or take up projects that are not profitable for us.
Before accepting an order, we evaluate its expected margin profile. Once an order is secured, our focus is on faster execution, disciplined budgeting and strong financial controls.
Our objective is not simply to generate revenue but to generate profitable revenue. That is the approach we have followed and will continue to follow.

Renewable energy companies are increasingly expanding beyond standalone solar into storage, transmission and hybrid projects. Will integrated renewable energy platforms have an advantage over pure-play solar companies?
Yes, that is correct. We recognised this opportunity and therefore entered the transmission and distribution EPC business.

Solar EPC and battery energy storage systems remain core areas for us, but we also need to expand into other segments that complement our existing operations and create value for shareholders and stakeholders.
We are continuously evaluating opportunities in areas where there are synergies with our existing businesses. The objective is to develop complementary capabilities and additional revenue streams.

What do the Q2 results indicate about the biggest bottlenecks in India's energy transition? Has the challenge shifted from adding renewable generation capacity towards transmission, storage and project execution?

The capacity addition numbers do not suggest that renewable energy growth is slowing. India installed more than 44 GW last year, and approximately 20 GW has already been added during the first half of the current financial year.

There are certainly constraints related to grid connectivity, transmission infrastructure, project delays, land availability and securing power purchase agreements. These are recurring challenges that developers must navigate.

However, these issues have not slowed the overall growth opportunity.  From our company's perspective, we have a strong order book, continue to receive new orders and maintain a substantial project pipeline. At present, we do not see anything suggesting an immediate slowdown in the sector.
